To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

RHOA missence mutations found in cancer are found at distinct hotspots than those of RAS, that these mutations are loss of function, and that they are found in a highly restricted subset of cancers, primarily in pancreatic and colon cancer.

RHOA is a tumor suppressor that functions in the control of cell proliferation and cell cycle progression and that RHOA mutations found in cancer are loss of function mutations that are found at a distinct mutational hotspots than those observed for RAC1 or RAS.

(i) RHOA missenses are found in a restricted range of cancer subtypes; (ii) RHOA mutants exhibit loss of function phenotypes in cell culture; (iii) RHOA mutations are found in human cancers that are characterized by loss of function mutations in other tumor suppressors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which RHOA mutations drive tumor progression, the identification of new cancer associated RHOA mutations and their functional characterization.
the role of RHOA in the pathogenesis and treatment of human cancer.
understanding the mechanisms that drive tumorigenesis in cancer and the role that GTPase signaling pathways play in cancer development and progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RHOA and the RAS GTPase family are not twins of the same mother, but rather twin brothers with a different mother.
RHOA mutations in cancer are a mixed bag of oncogene and tumor suppressor mutations, whereas the RAC1 mutations are clearly oncogenic.
the RHOA and the RAS mutations are not twin sons of the same mother.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RAS, RHO and RAC are twin sons of different biological mothers.
the cancer-associated RHOA mutations found in human cancer are not gain of function oncogenes.
the RAS and Rho family GTPases are twin sons of different mother, with distinct mutational signatures in cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RHOA mutations in cancer appear to be functionally diverse and have distinct biological consequences.
the RAS and RAC1 GTPases are oncogenic, whereas RHOA is a tumor suppressor in the context of cancer development.
the molecular mechanisms by which the RAS and RAC1 proteins promote oncogenic transformation are similar, whereas the mechanisms by which RHOA promotes cancer development are different.
